title: India Just Launched a Trade Probe That Could Sabotage Its Own ₹9-Lakh-Crore Power Grid.
excerpt: The government wants to protect steelmakers from Chinese dumping. But the steel in question goes into every transformer in the country — and India imports 90 percent of it.
body:
India's trade-enforcement machinery is moving in two directions at once — and they may be pulling the country's energy ambitions apart.

This week, the Directorate General of Trade Remedies (DGTR) launched not one but two anti-dumping investigations into steel imports. The first targets **hot-rolled flat steel** from China, Japan and Russia, after complaints by JSW Steel and Jindal Steel Odisha that cheap imports are undercutting domestic producers. China's finished steel exports to India more than doubled in April — to 232,000 metric tonnes — making it the country's top steel supplier and drawing alarm from domestic steelmakers.

The second probe is the one that has trade experts and energy planners genuinely worried.

It targets **Cold Rolled Grain Oriented (CRGO) electrical steel and Amorphous Metal** — the specialised magnetic alloy that sits inside the core of every power and distribution transformer in the country. The complaint was filed by JSW JFE Electrical Steel Nashik, a joint venture between JSW Steel and Japan's JFE Steel Corporation, and it names imports from China, Japan, South Korea and Russia.

The problem: India imports **nearly 90 percent** of its CRGO steel requirements. Domestic production meets only 40,000 to 50,000 tonnes against annual consumption of 400,000 to 450,000 tonnes. And demand is about to explode.

## The Power Grid Collision

India has committed **₹9.15 lakh crore** (roughly $108 billion) to expand its power grid by 2032. The plan calls for adding 191,000 circuit kilometres of transmission lines and more than doubling transformer capacity to 2,342 GVA. Every one of those transformers needs CRGO steel in its magnetic core — the grain-oriented crystalline structure is what minimises energy losses during electricity transmission.

"Imposing anti-dumping duties on a product for which India imports nearly 90 percent of its requirements could increase transformer costs and slow the country's ambitious power-grid expansion," warned Ajay Srivastava, founder of the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI) and a former Indian Trade Service officer.

The concern is not theoretical. Industry analysts estimate that CRGO steel accounts for 25 to 40 percent of the total cost of a distribution transformer. A duty of even 15 to 20 percent on imports — a typical range for anti-dumping measures — could add tens of thousands of crores to the national grid-expansion bill.

Transformer lead times are already stretching. What used to take six to eight months now runs 12 to 18 months in some categories. Solar parks are ready, but grid-connection transformers are not. DISCOM tenders are funded, but procurement pipelines are stalled. Rural electrification timelines are slipping.

## The Steelmaker's Case

JSW JFE has a legitimate grievance. As India's sole domestic CRGO producer, it argues that imports from four countries are arriving at prices below fair value, causing injury to the nascent domestic industry. The company — and its parent JSW Steel — have announced ₹5,845 crore in expansion plans to boost CRGO capacity from 50,000 to 350,000 tonnes per annum by FY2028, including a new 100,000-tonne facility at Vijayanagar.

If that expansion comes on schedule, India could move from 10 to 12 percent self-sufficiency to meeting a majority of domestic demand — a genuinely transformative shift. But it is a FY2028 answer to a 2026 problem.

Meanwhile, the hot-rolled steel probe has its own implications. China-India bilateral trade hit $151.1 billion in FY2026, with a record trade deficit of $112.6 billion. Chinese steel, cheaper by $11 to $37 per tonne than Indian equivalents, continues to lure buyers. Stainless steel MSMEs have separately urged the government to reinstate quality-control orders that were suspended in April, warning that a 65 percent year-on-year surge in stainless imports is threatening thousands of jobs.

## The Dilemma New Delhi Cannot Avoid

The twin probes expose a fault line that runs through Indian industrial policy: the tension between protecting domestic manufacturers and keeping infrastructure costs under control.

If DGTR recommends anti-dumping duties and the Finance Ministry imposes them, transformer manufacturers — who supply utilities, industrial users and renewable-energy projects — will pass on the higher costs. That ripples outward to state electricity boards, to industrial tariffs, and ultimately to consumers.

If the probes conclude without duties, India's only CRGO producer has less incentive to invest in capacity expansion, and the country remains import-dependent for a material the government itself has classified as strategic.

GTRI's Srivastava has also raised questions about the investigation's methodology, arguing that exporters from four different countries are being assessed against a common Indian cost benchmark — a practice he says may not adequately reflect varying production conditions across China, Japan, South Korea and Russia.

The DGTR investigations will determine whether dumping occurred, whether it caused material injury, and whether duties are warranted. The Finance Ministry makes the final call.

For now, India finds itself in a position familiar to fast-growing economies everywhere: it needs cheap imported inputs to build at scale, and it needs to protect the domestic capacity that would reduce that dependency. The answer to both cannot be the same policy.
